opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. So the motivation for ConvNeXt really came from a question we kept asking ourselves around 2021. At that point, Vision Transformers, and especially hierarchical ones like Swin Transformer, were outperforming ResNets on basically every benchmark: ImageNet classification, detection, segmentation. The common narrative was that this was because of self-attention, that attention was just fundamentally a better inductive bias, or rather a more flexible, less biased operator, than convolution.

But when you looked closely, the comparison wasn't really apples to apples. The transformer papers came with a whole package of changes beyond attention. They used a different training recipe, like AdamW, much longer training, heavy data augmentation such as Mixup, CutMix, and RandAugment, plus stochastic depth and label smoothing. They also had different macro-architecture choices: the patchify stem, the stage compute ratios, and different normalization and activation functions, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm and GELU instead of ReLU. Meanwhile, the ConvNet baselines people compared against were often ResNets trained with recipes from 2015 or 2016.

So what we did was essentially a controlled study. We started from a standard ResNet-50 and gradually "modernized" it, one step at a time, toward the design of a Swin Transformer, without ever introducing attention. At each step we measured the accuracy. The first big jump came just from the training recipe. Training a plain ResNet-50 with the modern transformer-style recipe already got you a couple of points on ImageNet. Then we went through the macro design: changing the stage ratios, using a patchify stem with a 4x4 non-overlapping convolution, using depthwise convolutions, which are kind of analogous to the per-channel mixing in attention, and an inverted bottleneck like in the transformer MLP block. We then increased the kernel size to 7x7 to get a larger receptive field, closer to the window size in Swin. And finally there were micro-level changes, like fewer activation and normalization layers, LayerNorm, GELU, and separate downsampling layers.

At the end of that process, we had a pure ConvNet, ConvNeXt, that matched or slightly outperformed Swin Transformers at similar FLOPs, on ImageNet and on downstream tasks like COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation, and it scaled reasonably well too.

So my takeaway is that a large part of the apparent gap was not about attention versus convolution per se. A lot of it came from the training techniques and the many design decisions that had accumulated in the transformer line of work and had simply never been applied to ConvNets. Once you control for those, the core operator matters less than people thought, at least at the scale of ImageNet-sized data and these model sizes.

That doesn't mean the architectures are identical in every respect. Transformers have real advantages in some settings: they're very natural for multimodal work, for handling tokens from different sources, and for certain kinds of scaling and masked pretraining. ConvNets have their own strengths in efficiency and simplicity, and in dense prediction at high resolution. But I think the broader lesson was methodological. When we compare architectures, we need to be careful to separate the effect of the architecture from everything else that comes along with it. Otherwise we risk attributing progress to the wrong thing.

r001.rationale: Describes a controlled study that modernized a ResNet toward Swin’s design while never adding attention, then measured performance. This communicates how other design choices were controlled to assess the operator’s effect.

r002.rationale: Attributes much of the gap to training techniques and accumulated architectural design decisions, and says the core operator matters less than previously thought.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. The short version is that when we actually looked carefully, the gap mostly wasn't about convolution versus attention. It was about everything else that changed around the same time.

When ViT came out, the comparison was a 2020 vision transformer against a 2015-era ResNet. The ResNet had an old training recipe, old design choices, old macro structure. The transformer came with a modern recipe: AdamW, long schedules, heavy augmentation like Mixup and CutMix, stochastic depth, label smoothing. So people saw a gap and attributed it to the architecture, when a lot of it was the recipe.

So in ConvNeXt we did something very deliberate. We started from a plain ResNet-50 and modernized it one step at a time, measuring ImageNet accuracy at each step. First we just applied the modern training recipe to the ResNet, and that alone gave something like two and a half points. Then we changed the stage compute ratio to match Swin. We replaced the stem with a patchify-style stem, a 4 by 4 non-overlapping convolution. We moved to depthwise convolutions and widened the network, which is essentially the ConvNet analogue of separating spatial mixing from channel mixing, like attention versus MLP in a transformer. We used an inverted bottleneck. We made the kernels bigger, 7 by 7. Then the micro design: GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activations, fewer normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, separate downsampling layers.

Each change is small, and individually none of them is a new idea. But stacked together, this pure ConvNet matched or beat Swin at every scale on ImageNet, and also on detection and segmentation, while being simpler and often faster in throughput.

So my reading is that the "gap" was largely a measurement artifact of comparing architectures from different eras under different conditions. Attention is a genuinely useful inductive bias, especially for scaling and multimodal settings, and I don't want to overclaim. But a lot of what looked like a transformer advantage was really the field collectively discovering better design principles, and those principles transfer to ConvNets just fine.

The broader lesson for me is about scientific hygiene. If you want to claim one architecture component matters, you need controlled comparisons where the recipe and the rest of the design are held fixed. Otherwise you end up attributing progress to the most visible change rather than the actual cause.

r001.rationale: The response calls for controlled comparisons with the recipe and the rest of the design held fixed to identify what causes performance differences.

r002.rationale: It attributes much of the apparent gap to differing training recipes and design choices, and says the gap was largely not about convolution versus attention.

astra-6.text:
The question we wanted to ask was: how much of that gap really comes from self-attention, and how much comes from all the other things that changed along the way? When we compare a vision transformer with a classic ResNet, we’re comparing architectures from different periods, often with different training recipes. So it’s difficult to attribute the improvement to one particular component.

In “A ConvNet for the 2020s,” we started with a ResNet and gradually modernized it, borrowing design choices from hierarchical vision transformers. We looked at things like the patch-like stem, larger convolution kernels, inverted bottlenecks, and the placement of normalization and activation layers. The resulting model, ConvNeXt, still uses standard convolutions, but it can compete very well with vision transformers on image classification and downstream tasks such as detection and segmentation.

To me, the takeaway is that the apparent gap wasn’t simply a fundamental limitation of convolution. A lot came from the surrounding architecture and training choices. That doesn’t mean attention has no advantages; it means that, to understand those advantages, we need a strong, modern convolutional baseline.

r001.rationale: The response notes that architectures and training recipes differ and describes modernizing a ResNet, but does not clearly say that other architectural components were controlled to isolate convolution versus self-attention.

r002.rationale: It says the gap was not a fundamental limitation of convolution and attributes much of it to surrounding architecture and training choices.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question we asked was: how much of that gap comes from the architecture itself, and how much comes from everything around it? When vision transformers became popular, people were often comparing them with ResNets that used older design choices and training recipes. So those comparisons didn’t necessarily isolate the benefit of attention.

In “A ConvNet for the 2020s,” we started with a standard ResNet and gradually modernized it, taking inspiration from the design of hierarchical vision transformers. We changed the training recipe, the stage structure, the stem, and the block design, including things like depthwise convolutions, larger kernels, and inverted bottlenecks. The result was ConvNeXt, a pure convolutional network that could compete very well with vision transformers in accuracy and efficiency, including on downstream tasks like detection and segmentation.

For me, the takeaway isn’t that attention is unnecessary or that convolutions are always better. It’s that the apparent gap was not simply a fundamental limitation of convolution. A lot of it came from design and training choices that had evolved more quickly for transformers. You need a strong, modern baseline before you can really understand what a new architectural component contributes.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier comparisons did not isolate attention’s benefit and describes modernizing ResNet, but it does not clearly say that other design components were controlled to isolate convolution versus self-attention.

r002.rationale: It says the gap was not a fundamental limitation of convolution and attributes much of it to design and training choices that had evolved faster for transformers.
